name: Branchless conditional accumulate (multiply by bool)
listed_description: Replace an unpredictable if (b) s += x with s += b*x so the CPU pipeline is not flushed by branch mispredictions.
claim_text: Branchless version reported at 498.89M items/s against 176.304M items/s for the conditional one, almost 3 times faster.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark micro-benchmark of f2(bool, unsigned long, unsigned long&) with unpredictable bool input; compiler, flags and CPU not stated in text; code in Chapter09 05_branch.C.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 9, section 'Optimization of conditional execution'

name: Preallocate-once buffer reuse (hoist new/delete out of loop)
listed_description: Allocate the maximum buffer once before the loop instead of calling new[] and delete[] on every iteration.
claim_text: Allocating every iteration runs at about 40% of the speed of the version that allocates the maximum size once.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, random string sizes up to 1 KB filled with memset, per-iteration new[]/delete[] versus one preallocated buffer; also run with 8 threads where the penalty is larger; figures only, hardware and flags not stated; code in Chapter09 04_buffer.C.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 9, section 'Unnecessary memory allocations'

name: Grow-only buffer (resize never shrinks)
listed_description: Simple buffer class that reallocates only when a larger size is requested and never releases memory until the work ends.
claim_text: Slower than a fixed preallocated buffer but much faster than allocating and deallocating every time.
book_benchmark: Same Google Benchmark as the fixed buffer case (random sizes up to 1 KB, single thread and 8 threads); only charts, no numeric values in the text; code in Chapter09 04_buffer.C.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 9, section 'Unnecessary memory allocations'

name: TCMalloc
listed_description: Popular malloc() replacement library using thread-local caches to avoid the global allocator lock in multi-threaded programs.
claim_text: Book gives no speedup for TCMalloc; it only says cross-thread deallocation with malloc or TCMalloc is at least an order of magnitude worse than thread-owned memory.
book_benchmark: Cross-thread deallocation benchmark mentioned in passing, no workload, compiler or CPU stated.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 9, section 'Memory management in concurrent programs'

name: Fixed-size block allocator (64 KB blocks with free list)
listed_description: Primary allocator hands out fixed 64 KB blocks carved from large 8 MB chunks, with per-thread free lists and secondary allocators on top; resists fragmentation and keeps recent blocks cache-hot.
claim_text: Application-specific allocators often bring dramatic performance improvements, at the cost of restricting data structure choices; no numbers given.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 9, section 'Avoiding memory fragmentation'

name: Sort a vector of pointers instead of copying large objects
listed_description: To print or process a sorted view of a vector of large objects, sort a vector of pointers with a dereferencing comparator instead of copying and sorting the objects.
claim_text: For integers copy-and-sort wins; for large objects the pointer indirection becomes relatively more efficient.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark print_sorted with printing disabled, fresh unsorted vector per iteration, vector of int versus vector of large objects, various sizes; figures only; code in Chapter09 01_vector_sort.C.
guessed_baseline: copy vector then std::sort of the elements
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 9, section 'Copying as an implementation technique'

name: Signed loop index in string comparison (compare2)
listed_description: Using a signed int loop index instead of unsigned int lets GCC use add instead of lea because signed overflow is undefined, speeding up a char-by-char string compare used for sorting.
claim_text: Signed-index compare2 was the best-performing version; the compiler assumption makes the entire sort several times faster than unsigned compare1.
book_benchmark: Sorting benchmark of a set of strings with compare1 (unsigned int) versus compare2 (int), GCC 9 x86-64 assembly inspected; flags and CPU not stated; figures only; code in Chapter11 04a_compare1.C and 04b_compare2.C.
guessed_baseline: same comparison loop with unsigned int index
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 11, section 'Undefined behavior and C++ optimization'

name: Compile-time specialization of runtime flags (template process/measure)
listed_description: Turn runtime configuration booleans into template parameters and dispatch once, so the compiler removes in-loop branches in each instantiation.
claim_text: Can yield substantial performance gains when millions of shapes get the same set of measurements; no numbers given.
guessed_baseline: single function with runtime flag checks inside the loop
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 10, section 'Lifting knowledge from runtime to compile time'

name: memset instead of byte-by-byte init loop
listed_description: Initialize two char arrays with std::memset rather than a loop writing one byte at a time; the compiler cannot make this change itself because the pointers may alias.
claim_text: The memset version will be much faster than the one-byte loop; no numbers given.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 10, section 'What does the compiler really know?'

name: std::deque traversal by iterator instead of index
listed_description: Iterating a std::deque with iterators lets the container reuse the block pointer instead of recomputing block and offset on every operator[] call.
claim_text: Traversal using an iterator is much faster than using an index; book calls the difference very impressive.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark over std::deque<unsigned long> of N elements, index loop versus iterator loop with DoNotOptimize; figure only; code in Chapter12 01_deque.C.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 12, section 'The maximum information principle'

name: index_tree with member find() scanning the data store
listed_description: Tree-like index of pointers into a vector data store; a member find() scans the contiguous vector directly in any order instead of walking the std::set index.
claim_text: Member find() is much faster than the iterator-based search, more pronounced when the value is not found or rare.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark of predicate search through the index_tree via set-order iterators versus member find() over the vector; figure only; code in Chapter12 02_index_tree.C.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 12, section 'The maximum information principle'
